results.question: According to IHL, when should the search for, collection, and evacuation of the dead be carried out?

options.A: Whenever circumstances permit, and particularly after an engagement, all parties involved in the conflict must, without delay, search for the dead, without adverse distinction.
options.B: After the general close of military operations, parties must employ all efforts to search for, collect and evacuate the dead.
options.C: After an engagement, every party to the conflict must collect its own dead, as every party is only responsible for the members of its own armed forces.
options.D: As soon as circumstances permit, especially after an engagement, all parties must search for the dead through all possible measures, including by allowing humanitarian organizations to do so.

Rule 112. Whenever circumstances permit, and particularly after an
engagement, each party to the conflict must, without delay, take all
possible measures to search for, collect and evacuate the dead without
adverse distinction.

Rule 109. Whenever circumstances permit, and particularly after an
engagement, each party to the conflict must, without delay, take all
possible measures to search for, collect and evacuate the wounded, sick
and shipwrecked without adverse distinction.

Rule 114. Parties to the conflict must endeavour to facilitate the return of the
remains of the deceased upon request of the party to which they belong or
upon the request of their next of kin. They must return their personal effects
to them.

Rule 117. Each party to the conflict must take all feasible measures to
account for persons reported missing as a result of armed conflict and must
provide their family members with any information it has on their fate.

Rule 113. Each party to the conflict must take all possible measures to
prevent the dead from being despoiled. Mutilation of dead bodies is prohibited.

Rule 139. Each party to the conflict must respect and ensure respect for
international humanitarian law by its armed forces and other persons or
groups acting in fact on its instructions, or under its direction or control.

Rule 116. With a view to the identification of the dead, each party to the
conflict must record all available information prior to disposal and mark the
location of the graves.

Rule 56. The parties to the conflict must ensure the freedom of movement
of authorised humanitarian relief personnel essential to the exercise of their
functions. Only in case of imperative military necessity may their
movements be temporarily restricted.

Rule 18. Each party to the conflict must do everything feasible to assess
whether the attack may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life,
injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects, or a combination thereof,
which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military
advantage anticipated.

Rule 159. At the end of hostilities, the authorities in power must endeavour
to grant the broadest possible amnesty to persons who have participated in a
non-international armed conflict, or those deprived of their liberty for reasons
related to the armed conflict, with the exception of persons suspected of,
accused of or sentenced for war crimes.

Rule 124.

A. In international armed conflicts, the ICRC must be granted regular access to
all persons deprived of their liberty in order to verify the conditions of their
detention and to restore contacts between those persons and their families.

B. In non-international armed conflicts, the ICRC may offer its services to the
patties to the conflict with a view to visiting all persons deprived of their
liberty for reasons related to the conflict in order to verify the conditions of
their detention and to restore contacts between those persons and their
families.

Rule 4. The armed forces of a party to the conflict consist of all organised
armed forces, groups and units which are under a command responsible to
that party for the conduct of its subordinates.

Rule 24. Each party to the conflict must, to the extent feasible, remove
civilian persons and objects under its control from the vicinity of military
objectives.

Rule 15. In the conduct of military operations, constant care must be taken to
spare the civilian population, civilians and civilian objects. All feasible
precautions must be taken to avoid, and in any event to minimise, incidental
loss of civilian life, injury to civilians and damage to civilian objects.

Rule 158. States must investigate war crimes allegedly committed by their
nationals or armed forces, or on their territory, and, if appropriate, prosecute
the suspects. They must also investigate other war crimes over which they
have jurisdiction and, if appropriate, prosecute the suspects.

results.question: Which of the following actions constitute violations of IHL?

options.A: Carrying the dead away from the place where they died, since they should be buried in the theatre of hostilities where they fell.

options.C: Despoiling the dead or pillaging their personal belongings, regardless of the objects' nature.
options.D: Mutilating the bodies of the deceased.

results.question: Do the parties to an conflict have to identify the dead under IHL?

options.A: Yes¨, and they need to deal respectfully with every deceased person, without adverse distinction.
options.B: Yes, being an obligation of result, failure by parties to a conflict to identify the dead is a violation of IHL.
options.C: No, the obligation to account for the dead is one of means and as such all parties must employ their best efforts and all means available to identify the dead.
options.D: Yes, however this is only an obligation for States. Given the limited resources of non-state actors, they must simply make every possible effort to identify the dead.

options.D: No, as this would give the detaining power an unfair military advantage. The only objects that can be kept as war booty are those with no military purpose.

results.question:
State Y and Z are engaged in an armed conflict. A soldier from State Y, wearing the camouflage uniform of his country’s
armed forces, is captured while gathering intelligence on State Z's troop movements. An interrogating officer from State Z tells the soldier that he will be treated as a spy and has no prisoner of war status. According to IHL, what treatment is the captured soldier entitled to?

options.A: If a soldier is captured while engaging in espionage behind enemy lines he loses prisoner of war status. The interrogating officer's judgement was correct.
options.B: Soldiers may use ruses to carry out their missions, and camouflage is a permitted ruse provided civilian clothing or the enemy uniform is not used during the intelligence gathering operation. The soldier is entitled to and must be treated as a prisoner of war.
options.C: A spy is one who gathers or attempts to gather intelligence within the zone of operations of a belligerent, secretly, under false pretences. Had the soldier not worn a camouflage uniform, he would have been entitled to prisoner of war status. However, he has forfeited this and can be treated as spy.
options.D: Members of the armed forces in uniform who obtain intelligence in the enemy zone of operation are not spies. The soldier's reconnaissance was a lawful combat activity and he is entitled to prisoner of war status upon capture.

results.question: Does respect for IHL depend on reciprocity?

options.A: Yes. Respect for IHL is subject to reciprocity, both in international and non-international armed conflicts.
options.B: No. IHL affirms that the obligation to respect and ensure respect for IHL does not depend on reciprocity in situations of international armed conflicts. In non-international armed conflicts, however, this obligation does depend on reciprocity.
options.C: Yes. Compliance with IHL depends on the capability of the party to do so. State actors have more resources to implement IHL than non-state actors, which means that the principle of reciprocity does not apply to non-international armed conflicts.
options.D: No. Respect for IHL by one party does not depend on respect for IHL by another. IHL must be respected in all circumstances.

results.question: Under IHL, is ensuring respect for IHL an erga omnes obligation?

options.A: No. The obligation to respect and ensure respect for IHL is exclusive to the parties to the conflict, as IHL regulates their behaviour during the duration of the armed conflict only, be it international or non-international.
options.B: No. States have no means to influence or control the behaviour of the parties to an armed conflict if their armed forces are not directly involved.
options.C: Yes. The obligation to ensure respect is not limited to the behaviour of parties to an armed conflict, but includes the requirement that States do everything in their power to ensure that IHL is respected universally.
options.D: Yes. State practice establishes this rule as a customary norm applicable in both international and non-international armed conflicts. International and regional organizations as well as international conferences support that States must call for respect of IHL even if they are not themselves directly involved in an armed conflict.

options.B: The definition of civilian objects has to be read together with the definition of military objectives: only those objects that qualify as military objectives may be attacked; other objects are protected against attack.
options.C: State practice considers civilian areas, towns, cities, villages, residential areas, dwellings, buildings and houses and schools, civilian means of transportation, hospitals, medical establishments and medical units, historic monuments, places of worship and cultural property, and the natural environment as prima facie civilian objects, provided they have not become military objectives in the final analysis.
options.D: Civilian objects are all objects that are not military objectives.

results.question: When do civilian objects lose protection from attack in an armed conflict?

options.A: Civilian objects lose their protection against attack until and for such time that they are military objectives.
options.B: Loss of protection of civilian objects must be read together with the basic rule that only military objectives may be attacked. It follows that when a civilian object is used in such a way that it loses its civilian character and qualifies as a military objective, it is liable to attack.
options.C: In case of doubt whether an object which is normally dedicated to civilian purposes, such as a place of worship or a school, is being used to make an effective contribution to military action, it can automatically be presumed to have lost its protection against attack.
options.D: The principle of presumption of civilian character of an object in case of doubt requires that it cannot automatically be assumed that any object that appears dubious may be subject to lawful attack, and that a careful assessment of the situation be made to determine if the object is being used to make an effective military contribution.

results.question: How are indiscriminate attacks regulated under IHL?

options.A: Indiscriminate attacks are permissible in the context of defensive military operations by a state against an invading force.

options.C: Indiscriminate attacks are always prohibited, in any armed conflict.
options.D: Indiscriminate attacks are generally prohibited in armed conflict, depending on the means and methods used.

results.question: How are indiscriminate attacks defined under IHL?

options.A: An indiscriminate attack does not include attacks that primarily affect the armed forces of the adversary.
options.B: The definition of indiscriminate attacks represents an application of the principle of distinction, the prohibition on attacking civilians and civilian objects, prohibition of weapons that are by nature indiscriminate, and prohibition of means and methods of warfare whose effects cannot be limited as required by IHL.
options.C: This definition of indiscriminate attacks does not apply in non-international armed conflicts.
options.D: The use of weapons whose effects are uncontrollable in time and space and are likely to strike military objectives and civilian objects without distinction is permissible based on the requirements of the prohibition on indiscriminate attacks.

results.question: To what extent is area bombardment prohibited in IHL?

options.A: Area bombardments are attacks by bombardment by any method or means which treat as a single military objective a number of clearly separated and distinct military objectives located in a city, town, village or other area containing a similar concentration of civilians or civilian objects, and are expressly prohibited.
options.B: The prohibition on area bombardments is applicable in international and non-international armed conflicts.
options.C: Area bombardments constitute a form of indiscriminate attack, and are prohibited.
options.D: An area bombardment is prohibited if it targets a location in which the majority of objects are military objectives, even if also destroying civilian objects.

results.question: In an armed conflict, what does abiding by the principle of proportionality in attack entail?

options.A: The principle of proportionality in attack prescribes that launching an attack which may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life, injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects, or a combination thereof, which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated, is prohibited.
options.B: If the overarching objective of an attack is to win the war, excessive civilian harm may be justified.
options.C: The principle of proportionality does not apply to attacks in non-international armed conflicts as Additional Protocol II does not contain an explicit reference to proportionality.
options.D: According to the International Criminal Court Statute, intentionally launching an attack with the knowledge that such attack will cause incidental loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian object which would be clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated constitutes a war crimes in international armed conflicts.

results.question: In an armed conflict, what does abiding by the principle of precautions in attack in entail?

options.A: The principle of precautions prescribes that in the conduct of military operations, constant care must be taken to spare the civilian population, civilians and civilian objects.
options.B: In the conduct of military operations, all feasible precautions must be taken to avoid, and in any event to minimize, incidental loss of civilian life, injury to civilians and damage to civilian objects. Feasible precautions have been defined by States and the Protocols to the CCW as those precautions which are practicable or practically possible, taking into account all circumstances ruling at the time, including humanitarian and military considerations.
options.C: The obligation to take precautions in non-international armed conflicts can be inferred from Article 13(1) of Additional Protocol II which requires that ‘the civilian population and individual civilians shall enjoy general protection against the dangers arising from military operations’.
options.D: When applying the principle of precautions, military commanders and those responsible for planning, deciding or executing attacks have to assess precautions based on relevant information from all sources available to them, including the best possible intelligence on concentrations of civilian persons, important civilian objects, specifically protected objects, the natural environment and the civilian environment of military objectives.

results.question: What does the IHL rule on target verification entail?

options.A: The rule on target verification is only binding on States in international armed conflicts.
options.B: The rule on target verification requires that parties to the conflict must do everything feasible to verify that targets are military objectives.
options.C: The precautions to be taken in targeting are equivalent to those to be respected in the choice of a military objective, where the attack may only be directed at and is limited to a specified military objective, which is identified as such and is clearly designated and assigned.
options.D: Once an objective is identified as a military objective, it can be lawfully attacked at any subsequent moment, even weeks later.

results.question: What does the IHL obligation to cancel or suspend an attack require?

options.A: Parties to the conflict must do everything feasible to cancel or suspend an attack if (a) it becomes apparent that the target is not a military objective or (b) that the attack may be expected to cause excessive incidental damage (loss of civilian life, injury to civilians, damage to civilian objects) in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.
options.B: Disregard for this rule may lead to a violation of the principles of distinction and proportionality.
options.C: This obligation comes into effect in a situation where the distinction, proportionality and precautionary assessments have been carried out and an attack has been planned or is underway, but it now becomes apparent that the target may not be a military objective or there may be excessive incidental damage, at which point as far as possible, the attack must be cancelled or suspended.
options.D: Once a military commander has identified a military objective and done a proportionality assessment, there is nothing that prevents attacking it.

results.question: What does the IHL obligation to give effective advance warning prior to an attack entail?

options.A: The concept of warnings is not explicitly mentioned in Additional Protocol II, and is therefore not applicable in non-international armed conflicts.

options.D: Even after a warning has been issued, all obligations related to distinction and conduct of hostilities remain applicable to protect civilians who may still remain in the zone of operations.

results.question: What does the IHL prohibition of torture entail?

options.A: Under IHL, torture is the intentional infliction, by act or omission, of severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, for such purposes as to obtain information or a confession, to punish, intimidate or coerce the victim or a third person, or to discriminate, on any ground, against the victim or a third person.

options.C: When distinguishing between torture and cruel/inhuman treatment, torture requires a higher threshold of pain or suffering, which must be ‘severe’ rather than ‘serious’, and the infliction of pain or suffering for torture must be the result of a specific purpose or motivation.
options.D: The prohibition of outrages upon personal dignity only applies to living persons.

results.question: How does IHL regulate the use of the distinctive emblems of the Geneva Convention, including the red cross and red crescent?

options.A: IHL prohibits the improper use of the distinctive emblems of the Geneva Conventions. These emblems may only be used to identify medical and religious personnel, medical units and transports, as well as personnel and property of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
options.B: The distinctive emblems of the Geneva Conventions have indicative and protective functions. As a protective device, the emblem is used to identify medical personnel, units and transports in times of armed conflict. As an indicative device, the emblem identifies persons, equipment and activities affiliated with the Red Cross or the Red Crescent.
options.C: Yes, the improper use of the distinctive emblems of the Geneva Conventions constitutes a war crime in international armed conflicts when those are being used by others outside of the ICRC.
options.D: The improper use of the distinctive emblems of the Geneva Conventions may constitute perfidy which is prohibited by IHL.

results.question: State A uses a truck displaying the red crescent to conduct military operations, resulting in the death of many civilians in State B. Which of the following statements is true?

results.question: State A conducts a military operation using the United Nations emblem and uniforms to decieve State B. Which of the following statements is true?

results.question: Does IHL prohibit the improper use of the protective emblem of cultural property?

options.A: Yes, the improper use of the protective emblem of cultural property is prohibited. This emblem is intended to identify and safeguard cultural heritage during armed conflicts, and its misuse can jeopardize the protection afforded to such properties.
options.B: Yes, because it is forbidden to misuse deliberately in armed conflict other internationally recognized protective emblems, including the emblem of cultural property.
options.C: No, because the improper use of the protective emblem of cultural property is not explicitly prohibited under Additional Protocols.
options.D: The use of such emblem is permitted by customary IHL. Only the improper use of ICRC emblems constitutes perfidy.

options.B: Non-hostile contact between parties to a conflict can only be through commanders. The parlementaire, if a combatant, would be a legitimate military target and may be captured or killed.
options.C: State B is under no obligation under IHL to respect or admit the parlementaire and therefore may feign respect for the note to capture and detain the parlementaire.
options.D: The importance of maintaining non-hostile contact between parties to an armed conflict resulted in the IHL rule obliging States that have received a request for such contact to accept that request, in good faith, and admit the authorised representative. Therefore, State B must respect and admit State A’s parlementaire.

options.B: No, "manifestly unlawful" orders are not always immediately recognizable as illegal, and subordinates are generally expected to follow orders, even if they appear questionable. Disobeying such orders is rarely an obligation.
options.C: No, manifestly unlawful orders and unlawful orders must both be disobeyed by subordinates. The only difference is that for unlawful orders, subordinates will bear the consequences of disobeying their commander's if it is proven that the order was in fact lawful.
options.D: Yes, the distinction between "manifestly unlawful" and "unlawful" orders implies that while combatants must disobey manifestly unlawful orders, there is less clarity on whether they must disobey orders that are simply unlawful, as interpretations vary across States.

Rule 57. Ruses of war are not prohibited as long as they do not infringe a rule

Rule 29. Medical transports assigned exclusively to medical transportation

Rule 140. The obligation to respect and ensure respect for international

Rule 33. Directing an attack against personnel and objects involved in a

Rule 12. Indiscriminate attacks are those:
